readings.title: Allergen information at a cafe
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A community cafe displayed ingredients on a board. Customers with allergies still asked staff because the recipe changed with seasonal supplies. The main obstacle was a board that did not match the current dish. One substitution appeared in the kitchen record but had not reached the counter. At first, the people involved did not agree on which part of the proposal deserved the most attention.

To investigate, the team used a review of recipe changes and handovers. The manager traced how information moved from cooks to servers without asking customers to take risks. The organizers kept the first stage small enough to change without wasting substantial time or resources.

The evidence indicated a dated update process was essential. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced current ingredient sheets confirmed before service. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. The records were useful because they described ordinary use rather than an ideal situation imagined at a meeting.

The case suggests a broader point: food information must reflect what is actually served. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. The group published its reasons so that people who preferred a different result could still understand the choice. For those taking part in allergen information at a cafe, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records.

readings.title: Serving breakfast at a school
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A school offered a morning breakfast. Many pupils arrived at once, and some left before eating because the line moved slowly. The main obstacle was one queue for food and registration. Children who only needed a simple item waited behind those asking questions about the menu. The question mattered to people with different schedules and levels of experience, so one account could not represent everyone.

To investigate, the team used arrival-time counts and staff observations. The school recorded when pupils joined and where the line stopped. A simple record of what happened each day gave the team a starting point for comparison.

The evidence indicated separating the two tasks shortened waits. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced a quick collection point beside the registration desk. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. Some participants welcomed the change immediately, while others noticed practical details that needed further work.

The case suggests a broader point: a useful service must fit a short morning window. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. The result was a revised plan, not a claim that every difficulty had disappeared. For those taking part in serving breakfast at a school, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

readings.title: A recipe card for shared kitchens
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A housing group prepared recipe cards for a shared kitchen. Beginners reported that some cards used measures they could not reproduce. The main obstacle was instructions based on vague amounts. Phrases such as a little water meant different things to people with different cooking experience. The initial idea sounded reasonable, yet the details of the place made it harder to carry out than expected.

To investigate, the team used a cooking session with first-time readers. Volunteers followed the card exactly and noted every step that required guessing. Instead of relying on a single opinion, the team invited several users to describe what they actually did.

The evidence indicated specific amounts improved repeatability. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced revised cards with clear measures and photographs. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. This allowed the organizers to separate a temporary inconvenience from a pattern that required attention.

The case suggests a broader point: practical instructions should work for newcomers. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. They also decided when to check the arrangement again, because conditions could change over time. For those taking part in a recipe card for shared kitchens, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

readings.title: Reducing lunch waste at a college
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A college dining hall threw away many side dishes. Staff assumed portions were too large, but students often wanted a different choice. The main obstacle was waste figures without reasons for rejection. The bin count did not show whether food had been taken automatically or chosen willingly. The people affected were invited to comment before a permanent arrangement was chosen.

To investigate, the team used a short trial of optional side portions. The team recorded uptake and waste while inviting anonymous student comments. The first trial produced both useful results and questions the team could not yet answer.

The evidence indicated choice reduced unwanted servings. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced smaller default sides with a free request for more. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. Rather than hide those limits, the public note explained how the next version had been selected.

The case suggests a broader point: waste decisions need evidence about behaviour. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. That explanation made later changes easier to discuss with residents and staff. For those taking part in reducing lunch waste at a college, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

translation.stem:
Translate the following passage into Chinese:
Projects concerning nutrition information and community food often begin with a practical question. People may agree on a general goal while experiencing the same service in different ways. In this case, local organizers invited residents to describe ordinary visits and kept simple records of what happened. They compared those accounts before changing the community food information programme. The first trial did not answer every question, but it showed which difficulties were repeated and which were temporary. Staff then explained the reasons for a modest adjustment. Clear information helped people understand the decision, including those who would have preferred another option. The group planned to review the arrangement again after more people had used it.

translation.referenceAnswer: 有关营养信息与公共餐饮的项目通常从一个实际问题开始。人们可能赞同总体目标，却对同一服务有不同体验。在这个案例中，当地组织者请居民描述日常使用情况，并简单记录发生的事情。他们对照这些叙述后调整了服务。最初的试行无法回答所有问题，但能显示哪些困难反复出现，哪些只是暂时现象。工作人员随后解释了一项适度调整的原因。清楚的信息帮助人们理解决定，包括那些更希望采用其他方案的人。团队计划在更多人使用后再次评估安排。

writing.stem: Write at least 100 words in English to the community nutrition team proposing a small improvement to the community food information programme. Explain the problem, describe a short trial, and say what evidence should guide the final decision.
writing.explanation: 范文供考生自评，注意任务要点、组织结构及语言准确性。
writing.sampleAnswer:
Dear Committee Members,
I would like to propose a small improvement to the community food information programme. People have noticed a board that did not match the current dish, and a short trial could help us understand how often this problem occurs. We should ask regular users and people who have not used the service before to describe their experiences. Their comments may reveal details that a plan made in an office would miss.
For one month, staff could keep a simple record of participation, time spent and any difficulties reported. We should also explain the purpose of the trial in clear language so that residents know how to contribute. After the month, please publish a brief summary of both benefits and limits. The final decision should be based on what people actually experienced, with a date for checking the arrangement again.
Yours sincerely,
A resident
